source.text: וַ/תִּקַּ֨ח צִפֹּרָ֜ה צֹ֗ר וַ/תִּכְרֹת֙ אֶת עָרְלַ֣ת בְּנָ֔/הּ וַ/תַּגַּ֖ע לְ/רַגְלָ֑י/ו וַ/תֹּ֕אמֶר כִּ֧י חֲתַן דָּמִ֛ים אַתָּ֖ה לִֽ/י־־׃

translation.text: Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched his feet[a] with it[b], and she said, “Surely you are a bridegroom of blood[c] to me.”

footnotes.text: The possessor of 'his feet' is not named. Moses, the son, or the divine attacker have been proposed; 'feet' may also be a euphemism for genitals. None is specified in the main text.

The Hebrew says that she caused contact at his feet, without an explicit object corresponding to 'it'; the English infers the cut foreskin. The selected Greek text instead describes her falling toward the feet, without naming their owner.

The exact sense and addressee of 'bridegroom of blood' are uncertain. The selected Greek text has a different declaration about the child's circumcision blood; that is an alternative versional form, not the wording of this Hebrew phrase.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes flint/stone used as a cutting implement. 'Flint' is the most natural concise English rendering and fits the circumcision context.
A direct, anatomically precise rendering of the construct phrase; no euphemizing beyond normal English style.

lexical_decisions.lexicon: WLC/OSHB source analysis and bounded published-source comparison
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source analysis is Hiphil wayyiqtol3fs of נגע, causing contact. English touched ... with it infers the cut foreskin as an implicit object; the note makes this supply visible. Greek falling toward the feet is a different action, not an equivalent gloss.

lexical_decisions.lexicon: WLC/OSHB source analysis and bounded published-source comparison
lexical_decisions.rationale: Feet has a masculine possessor suffix but no named possessor. Retain that uncertainty and disclose proposed human/divine referents and possible euphemism, without asserting an exclusive interpretation.
Here כִּי introduces Zipporah's exclamation. 'Surely' captures the emphatic/exclamatory force better than a wooden 'for' in modern English.

alternatives: a relative by marriage of blood
lexical_decisions.lexicon: WLC/OSHB source analysis and bounded published-source comparison
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retain the unusual construct phrase without deciding cultural meaning or addressee. The selected Greek circumcision-blood declaration is separately disclosed, not blended into this Hebrew wording.
The preposition marks personal relation. 'To me' is idiomatic with the retained nominal expression 'a bridegroom of blood.'

theological_decisions.issue: Whether to resolve the ambiguity of 'his feet' as a euphemism or identify the referent explicitly as Moses or the son
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Retain the literal wording 'his feet' without specifying beyond the Hebrew text
theological_decisions.rationale: Retain unnamed possessor and feet without resolving possible euphemism. Human and divine referents are proposals, not explicit wording; distinguish Greek falling from Hebrew causing contact.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Translation philosophy §3 (Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it)

value.text: Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched his feet with it[a], and she said, “Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me.”

footnotes.text: Hebrew 'his feet.' 'Feet' may be a euphemism for genitals, and the pronoun may refer to Moses or to her son.

value.rationale: The noun denotes flint/stone used as a cutting implement. 'Flint' is the most natural concise English rendering and fits the circumcision context.
A direct, anatomically precise rendering of the construct phrase; no euphemizing beyond normal English style.
The verb נגע normally means 'touch, reach, strike.' 'Touched' preserves the verbal simplicity and leaves the exact manner of contact unspecified.

The plain lexical sense is 'his feet.' Because 'feet' can function as a euphemism in Hebrew, the alternative is preserved in a footnote rather than imported into the main text. The pronoun's referent is also debated, but the Hebrew itself simply reads 'his feet.'
Here כִּי introduces Zipporah's exclamation. 'Surely' captures the emphatic/exclamatory force better than a wooden 'for' in modern English.

alternatives: a relative by marriage of blood
value.rationale: This is an unusual and difficult expression. 'Bridegroom of blood' preserves the Hebrew imagery and ambiguity more transparently than smoothing it into an interpretive paraphrase.
The preposition marks personal relation. 'To me' is idiomatic with the retained nominal expression 'a bridegroom of blood.'
